extracted.intended_audience: appellate attorneys / petitioners (Supreme Court), litigators in federal voting-rights and election-contest cases
extracted.subtask_description: A petition to the U.S. Supreme Court seeking review of lower-court rulings on Section 5 (preclearance) Voting Rights Act claims and on the constitutionality and application of a state bond-posting statute in election-contest litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 preclearance requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in voting procedures in covered jurisdictions must be submitted for preclearance under Section 5 (42 U.S.C. §1973c) before implementation; preclearance is a stringent, prospective requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutory language and Supreme Court decisions (McCain v. Lybrand, Allen v. State Board of Elections, N.A.A.C.P. v. Hampton County). Emphasizes that the preclearance requirement 'prohibits jurisdictions ... from implementing any election practices different from those in effect on November 1, 1964 pending scrutiny by Federal Officials' and that timely, voluntary submission before implementation is 'the crucial threshold element of compliance.' Senate report quoted to show legislative intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of preclearance submission
rubrics_metrics.description: A submission to the Attorney General must be made before the election or change is implemented; post-election submissions do not satisfy Section 5's requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses NAACP v. Hampton County (timely submission is crucial), factual examples from the case (elections held August 10 and November 2, 1985; submissions received December 9, 1985 and February 14, 1986). Argues that allowing post-clearance would nullify Section 5 enforcement because jurisdictions could hold elections then seek clearance after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and scope of a submission for preclearance
rubrics_metrics.description: A submission that fails to identify particular changes cannot be treated as adequate for those unmentioned changes; ambiguities in scope are resolved against the submitting jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and paraphrase from McCain v. Lybrand and Perkins v. Mathews: 'A request for pre-clearance for certain identified changes ... which fails to identify other practices ... cannot be considered an adequate submission on the latter practice.' If only some practices are described (e.g., student ratios but not general population or voting-effect), those omitted practices remain un-cleared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Attorney General's 'no objection' or failure to object
rubrics_metrics.description: An Attorney General letter stating he 'interposes no objections' or the Attorney General's failure to object does not bar a subsequent private action to enjoin enforcement of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes statutory text (42 U.S.C. §1973c): 'Neither an affirmative indication by the Attorney General that no objection will be made, nor the Attorney General's failure to object, nor a declaratory judgment entered under this section shall bar a subsequent action to enjoin enforcement ...' Court should not treat post-election 'no objections' letters as dispositive of private suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-judge court requirement for Section 5 cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has required that certain voting-rights/preclearance cases be heard by a Three-Judge Court rather than a single judge; a single judge lacks authority to rule finally on the merits of those Section 5 claims when the statute requires a three-judge panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that the trial judge erred in failing to convene a Three-Judge Court and in deciding the merits; cites precedent indicating that when approval provisions of the Voting Rights Act are implicated, a three-judge court must decide coverage questions (citing case law such as Saint Landry Parish School Bd. discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-judge dismissal restraint where three-judge panel required
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-judge court cannot summarily dismiss Section 5 claims as 'without merit' and thereby avoid convening the Three-Judge Court if statutory or precedential rules require multi-judge consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the trial court's statement that a three-judge panel could not 'hold the elections void' was improper; a trial judge may not preclude relief that a Three-Judge Panel or higher court could grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete submission does not clear unsubmitted items
rubrics_metrics.description: If a submission identifies some changes but omits others, the omitted changes are not precleared by implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites McCain v. Lybrand and related precedents: 'to the extent there was any ambiguity in the scope of the pre-clearance request, the structure and purpose ... counsel against resolving such ambiguities in favor of the submitting jurisdiction.' Applied to facts where only one absentee item (judge qualification) was cleared but nine other alleged variations were never submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims survive facial dismissal if pleadings state plausible facts (Rule 12(b)(6) standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, the complaint must be construed in the plaintiff's favor, taking well-pleaded factual allegations as true; dismissal is improper if any set of facts could entitle plaintiff to relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Conley v. Gibson, In re Longhorn Securities Litigation, U.S. v. Howell: courts must accept well-pleaded facts, draw reasonable inferences for plaintiffs, and disregard unsupported legal conclusions. Quotation: 'A complaint should not be dismissed for failure to state a claim unless it appears beyond doubt that the Plaintiff can prove no set of facts ... which would entitle him to relief.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for determining whether a federal claim is 'insubstantial'
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal claim is 'unsubstantial' only if its soundness so clearly results from prior Supreme Court decisions as to foreclose any controversy (Goolsby/Goolsby-derived standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Goolsby v. Osser and Pine Township Citizens Assoc. explanation: 'its soundness so clearly results from the previous decisions of this Court as to foreclose the subject and leave no room for the inference that the questions sought to be raised can be the subject of controversy.' Used to argue the federal questions here are substantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation or annexation requiring preclearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that alter the size or composition of the electorate — e.g., consolidation of school districts or annexation — are potentially subject to Section 5 preclearance because they may affect minority voting strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites N.A.A.C.P. v. Hampton County and Perkins v. Mathews: consolidation/annexation have the potential for discrimination and therefore must be submitted for preclearance; factual focus on minority percentages in the separate districts (e.g., 19% vs. 3%).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of specific election-procedure statutory requirements (state law standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific state election-code requirements that, if violated, constitute procedural irregularities: absentee voting location availability, notice posting timelines, absentee voting start times, filing/copying/public posting of notices, judge/clerk qualifications and relation restrictions, physical custody and delivery of ballots/returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates V.A.T.S. Election Code provisions cited in the petition (Art. 5.05 subdivisions re: absentee voting, Art. 4.05 on notice, Art. 3.03 on judge/clerk qualifications and relations, Art. 8.32 on returns delivery, Art.19.004(e) on posting). The brief itemizes ten alleged deviations from these statutes and notes only one was addressed in the AG letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations and admitted facts on motion to dismiss are taken as true
rubrics_metrics.description: Where defendants' pleadings admit facts, or plaintiffs properly plead facts, those admissions/pleadings must be accepted as true when deciding a 12(b)(6) motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to this case where the respondent's pleadings admitted (1) only one absentee voting place, (2) absentee voting not held 20 days prior, (3) absentee clerk related to district employee, (4) absentee clerk non-resident — the petition argues these admissions require denial of dismissal and allow a full merits presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory protection vs. private suits (no absolute bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute's mechanisms (AG clearance or declaratory judgments) do not create an absolute bar to subsequent private litigation seeking to enjoin enforcement of the challenged practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates statutory sentence from 42 U.S.C. §1973c and cites cases interpreting that a 'no objection' from AG does not extinguish private rights to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 717m-1 bond mechanism and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Texas Rev. Civ. Stat. art. 717m-1 permits a public agency to require opposing parties/intervenors to post a bond to cover damages and costs attributable to delay caused by litigation, payable if agency ultimately prevails; statutory aim is to prevent a single litigant from stalling bond issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes statute language and Buckholts Independent School District v. Glaser: legislative purpose is to protect public projects from delay costs and to prevent 'one disgruntled taxpayer' from stopping an issue. Explains procedural operation (motion, hearing, bond amount fixed by court, 10-day deadline to post).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a court must set a damage bond under art. 717m-1
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should require a bond unless there is an absence of credible evidence of prospective damage, or other statutory reasons (e.g., indigency may be relevant); if evidence shows some likelihood of damage (e.g., expected bond issues and likely interest-rate increases) a bond is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains appellate modification requiring bond where the City produced evidence (likelihood $200M issued within year, likely 1–2% interest increase, probable delay of about a year) and trial court erred in refusing bond. Cites appellate reasoning that calculation may be speculative but is authorized by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation factors for bond amount under art. 717m-1
rubrics_metrics.description: Bond amount is based on damages and costs attributable to delay, including anticipated increases in interest rates, construction and financing costs; court may allocate bond among multiple opposing parties according to degree of participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory text allows the court to receive evidence on anticipated interest increases, construction/financing cost increases, and to allocate bond among participants. Appellate court set bond by reference to lowest potential loss supported by record and reduced to present value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indigency and bond constitutionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigency does not automatically exempt a litigant from bond requirements; courts evaluate the statute under rational-basis scrutiny and consider alternate avenues of relief for indigents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Boddie v. Connecticut, Kras, Ortwein, Lindsey v. Normet: bond provisions are constitutional if they rationally further a legitimate state interest; indigent litigants retain alternatives (requirement only if they cannot show entitlement to preliminary injunction; appeal available).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failing to post bond (jurisdictional and preclusive consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to post the statutory bond within the prescribed time results in dismissal and may deprive appellate courts of jurisdiction to consider issues that were or could have been raised in the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites art. 717m-1 §8 and subsequent case law (Buckholts, Rio Grande Valley Sugar Growers): dismissal for failure to post bond is final and precludes further litigation of the issues unless timely appeal or bond posting occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for what constitutes substantial federal question for federal court to hear pendent state claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A pendent state-law claim may be heard only if the federal question is not 'insubstantial'; if federal claims are substantial (not foreclosed by prior decisions) the federal court may exercise jurisdiction over pendent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses Pine Township and Goolsby tests; argues the denial of federal jurisdiction here was improper because the voting-procedure changes are federal issues requiring Three-Judge Court consideration and the due-process question re: art. 717m-1 raises a substantial federal constitutional question.
